title: Water conservation and environmental release
audience: Pool technicians and cleaners who drain, backwash, top up or discharge pool water, in any state or territory
learningOutcomes: Explain why unplanned loss of pool water raises cost and chemical use
Identify the discharge options set by the water authority, council and operator plan for drained, backwash and overflow water
Refuse to release pool water to stormwater or the environment without an approved route
Record water volumes, discharge routes and approvals

instruction.heading: Why water loss costs money
instruction.body: Pool water is expensive to replace. Every litre lost to splash-out, evaporation, leaks, or unnecessary backwashing must be topped up with mains water and re-treated with chemical. Losses also upset the chemical balance, so a top-up can change pH and sanitiser levels. Cost reduction starts with finding the cause of loss rather than topping up. Check whether the loss matches evaporation on a hot still day or whether it suggests a leak or a backwash that is run too often.

instruction.heading: Finding leaks and unnecessary backwashing
instruction.body: A simple bucket test helps separate evaporation from a leak. Place a bucket filled to the same level on the top step, and mark the water level inside and outside the bucket over the same period. If the pool drops more than the bucket, the loss is more likely a leak or an outlet problem, and it should be reported. Backwash only when the filter pressure reading and the operator plan indicate that it is needed, and record the reading that triggered it. Backwashing more often than needed wastes water and chemical and adds to the discharge volume.

instruction.heading: Discharge routes are set by the authority
instruction.body: Where pool water must be removed, the route depends on the local water authority, the council, the state or territory rules, and the operator plan. There is no single national route. Unitywater's domestic pool wastewater policy in South East Queensland is used here as one example. The policy (reviewed 16 July 2025, amended March and April 2026) accepts maintenance water to sewer only as a last option, when garden reuse cannot be done safely or sensibly, and caps that discharge at 0.5 L/s within two windows, 10am to 5pm and 10pm to 5am. It keeps rainwater overflow out of the sewer unless every other option has been ruled out as unsafe or unworkable, and it points to private stormwater drains, garden storage or a seepage option first. A sewer discharge needs written approval from the authority. The Icon Water acceptance guideline for pools in the ACT (version dated August 2016) is a different example: it allows a domestic pool to go to sewer only in limited cases, and says rainwater overflow must stay out of the sewer. Both are examples for one authority each, not state-wide rules.

instruction.heading: Chlorine, stormwater and waterways
instruction.body: Do not assume that chlorine has evaporated or been used up because a reading is low. The discharge route must be confirmed with the operator, the council and the water authority before any water is moved. The Unitywater policy sets no chlorine limit and describes no dechlorination method. The Icon Water guideline sets a total chlorine ceiling of 5 mg/L as Cl and a pH range of 6.5 to 10.0 for the discharges it covers, rules out sodium thiosulfate as a dechlorinating agent, and says rinse water from acid or strong-detergent cleaning must not go to sewer. Do not invent a dechlorination method; use the one the site's authority states.

instruction.heading: Recording water movements
instruction.body: Record the volume drained or backwashed where it is known, the route, the authority or approval relied on, the time, the reason, and the operator who approved the discharge. Where the discharge route is unknown, stop and refer. Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan, and the plan may restrict when water can be moved and how it is treated before discharge.

procedure: Check the reason for the water loss, including a bucket test where the cause is unclear.
Record the filter pressure and backwash trigger before any backwash.
Confirm the discharge route with the operator, the council and the water authority before moving water.
If the route is approved, drain or backwash within the stated limits and at the stated times.
Do not discharge to stormwater or waterways without an approved route and written confirmation.
Record the volume where known, the route, the approval and the operator who approved it.
Report any leak or unexpected loss to the operator and refer the repair.

workedExamples.situation: A homeowner asks you to drain the pool onto the front lawn and into the kerb drain because the chlorine will evaporate.
workedExamples.reasoning: The discharge route must be confirmed before water is moved. The worker does not drain to the kerb drain on the homeowner's assumption. The worker checks the council and the water authority rules, offers the route the authority allows, such as reuse on the garden where that is approved, records the request and the decision, and does not treat the chlorine loss as a reason to discharge.

workedExamples.situation: A pool loses a noticeable amount of water each night while the weather is still and cool.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the technician do first?
workedExamples.reasoning: The technician carries out a bucket test and records the drop. The loss is more consistent with a leak or outlet problem than with evaporation on a cool still night. The technician reports the finding to the operator and refers the leak check rather than topping up repeatedly.

equipmentAndPpe: Bucket and marker for bucket test
Discharge approval or written route confirmation

commonErrors.error: Draining to stormwater or the kerb without an approved route.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the route with the operator, council and water authority first.

commonErrors.error: Assuming chlorine evaporates and is safe to discharge.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not assume. Confirm the requirement for the site.

commonErrors.error: Backwashing on a timer rather than on the pressure trigger.
commonErrors.prevention: Backwash on the recorded trigger and within the plan.

commonErrors.error: Topping up repeatedly without finding a leak.
commonErrors.prevention: Run a bucket test and report a suspected leak.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: In Queensland, Unitywater's domestic pool policy requires written approval for some discharges to sewer and sets a 0.5 L/s maximum for maintenance water, with set time windows. In the ACT, Icon Water's guideline (August 2016) sets total chlorine and pH limits for the discharges it covers.
Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan.
Pool water containing chemicals can harm plants, animals and waterways, so do not release it without an approved route.

qualityStandard: Discharge route confirmed in writing before water is moved
Filter pressure trigger and backwash decision recorded
Volumes and approvals recorded where known
documentationEvidence: Bucket test record where loss is investigated
summary: Find the cause of water loss before topping up.
Backwash on the recorded pressure trigger, not on habit.
Confirm the discharge route with the operator, council and water authority before moving water.
Do not discharge pool water to stormwater or waterways without an approved route.

knowledgeChecks.question: A homeowner wants pool water drained into the kerb drain. What must happen first?
options: Drain it quickly before the chlorine is noticed by the neighbours or the council
Assume chlorine has evaporated, so it is safe to drain it into the kerb drain today
Confirm the approved discharge route with the operator, council and water authority
Ask the neighbour whether it is fine to drain it into their own gutter today

knowledgeChecks.question: A pool loses water every night in still, cool weather. What is the best first step?
options: Top it up every night without investigating
Backwash the filter straight away to fix the loss
Drain half the pool and refill it with fresh water
Run a bucket test and report a suspected leak

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is a backwash on a fixed timer not a good practice?
options: It can waste water and chemical when the filter does not need it
It always uses too little water to clean the filter properly
It stops the pump working when the filter is full and needs a clean
It changes the pool colour over the weekend for every swimmer
